```js
      100, "#bd0026",
    ],
    "fill-opacity": 0.75,
    "fill-outline-color": "#ffffff",
  },
});
```

### maps-react

```jsx
<Source id="areas" type="geojson" data="/data/areas.geojson">
  <Layer
    id="areas-fill"
    type="fill"
    paint={{
      "fill-color": [
        "interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "value"],
        0, "#ffffcc",
        50, "#fd8d3c",
        100, "#bd0026",
      ],
      "fill-opacity": 0.75,
      "fill-outline-color": "#ffffff",
    }}
  />
</Source>
```

Reading the `interpolate` expression:

1. `["linear"]`: interpolate linearly between values.
2. `["get", "value"]`: take `properties.value` of each polygon.
3. The rest are value and colour pairs. `0` is pale yellow, `100` is deep red, and everything between varies continuously.

Keeping `fill-opacity` below 1 lets the map underneath, roads and place names, show through so the location stays legible.

**When it does not work**

- Everything is the same colour: check the spelling of the property name and that the value is a **number**. A string such as `"72"` disables the expression.
- Some areas turn blackish: those polygons have a **missing** property. Fill it in the data or give a default with something like `["coalesce", ["get", "value"], 0]`.
- Nothing appears: check for a missing `Layer` `id`, or a 404 on the GeoJSON.

---

## Visualise Density with a Heatmap

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/howto/heatmap/

When there are too many points for individual markers to mean anything, a heatmap shows **where they concentrate** through shading. Use markers or clustering to show individual points, and a heatmap to show the shape of the distribution.

### embed

Not available with HTML attributes alone. Switch to the maps-suite or maps-react code.

### maps-suite

```js
await map.whenReady();
const impl = map.getGeoloniaMap();
impl.addSource("pts", { type: "geojson", data: "/data/dense-points.geojson" });
impl.addLayer({
  id: "heat",
  type: "heatmap",
  source: "pts",
  paint: {
    "heatmap-weight": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "weight"], 0, 0, 6, 1],
    "heatmap-intensity": 1,
    "heatmap-radius": 20,
    "heatmap-opacity": 0.8,
    "heatmap-color": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["heatmap-density"],
      0, "rgba(0,0,255,0)",
      0.2, "royalblue",
      0.4, "cyan",
      0.6, "lime",
      0.8, "yellow",
      1, "red",
    ],
  },
});
```

### maps-react

```jsx
<Source id="pts" type="geojson" data="/data/dense-points.geojson">
  <Layer
    id="heat"
    type="heatmap"
    paint={{
      "heatmap-weight": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "weight"], 0, 0, 6, 1],
      "heatmap-intensity": 1,
      "heatmap-radius": 20,
      "heatmap-opacity": 0.8,
      "heatmap-color": [
        "interpolate", ["linear"], ["heatmap-density"],
        0, "rgba(0,0,255,0)",
        0.2, "royalblue",
        0.4, "cyan",
        0.6, "lime",
        0.8, "yellow",
        1, "red",
      ],
    }}
  />
</Source>
```

There are mainly four things to tune.

- **`heatmap-weight`**: the weight of one point. The example converts each point `weight` property, running 0 to 6, into 0 to 1. Treating every point equally means a fixed `1`.
- **`heatmap-radius`**: the radius in pixels one point influences. Larger spreads more smoothly.
- **`heatmap-intensity`**: overall strength. Raising it with zoom keeps the shading as you zoom in.
- **`heatmap-color`**: density, running 0 to 1, mapped to colour. Making density 0 transparent is the usual choice.

**When it does not work**

- Barely any colour: few points means low density. Try raising `heatmap-radius` or `heatmap-intensity`.
- It fades away as you zoom in: higher zoom spreads the points and lowers density. Either raise `heatmap-intensity` with zoom, or switch to a `circle` layer at high zoom to show individual points.
- Nothing appears: check for a missing `Layer` `id`, or a 404 on the GeoJSON.

---

## Show Buildings and Terrain in 3D

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/howto/3d/

3D buildings are **included in the Geolonia standard style from the start**. Turn them on with the setting each library provides, tilt the viewpoint, and the city appears in three dimensions. Building shapes and heights come from the vector tiles, so there is no style and no data to prepare.

Only the way to enable them differs. embed disables them by default and needs them turned on explicitly, maps-suite enables them by default, and maps-react disables them by default.

### embed

Add `data-3d="on"`. The viewpoint is tuned with `data-pitch` (tilt) and `data-bearing` (rotation).

```html
<div class="geolonia"
     data-lat="35.6812" data-lng="139.7671" data-zoom="15.5"
     data-pitch="60" data-bearing="-20"
     data-3d="on"></div>
```

`data-3d="on"` switches on the 3D building layer built into the standard style. It only takes effect while using a Geolonia style that contains 3D buildings, so it does nothing if `data-style` points at an external style.

### maps-suite

3D buildings are **enabled by default**, so tilting the viewpoint is enough. There is no layer to add. Tilt is `tilt` and rotation is `heading`, both in degrees, and both changeable afterwards with `map.setTilt()` and `map.setHeading()`.

```js
const map = new geolonia.maps.Map(document.getElementById("map"), {
  apiKey: "YOUR-API-KEY",
  center: { lat: 35.6812, lng: 139.7671 },
  zoom: 15.5,
  tilt: 60,
  heading: -20,
});
```

Passing `threeDimensional: false` keeps buildings flat even when tilted.

### maps-react

3D buildings are disabled by default, so pass `3d` to enable them. The name begins with a digit and therefore cannot be written as a JSX attribute; pass it through an object spread. The viewpoint uses `pitch` and `bearing`.

```jsx
<Map
  apiKey="YOUR-API-KEY"
  center={[139.7671, 35.6812]}
  zoom={15.5}
  pitch={60}
  bearing={-20}
  {...{ "3d": true }}
  containerStyle={{ width: "100%", height: "100vh" }}
/>
```

**When it does not work**

- No buildings: check whether you specified an external style. 3D buildings belong to the Geolonia styles, so replacing the style removes them.
- They disappear when zoomed out: buildings are drawn only from the zoom level at which they carry meaning. This is intended.
- maps-react will not enable them: `3d={true}` cannot be written. Check that you are passing `{...{ "3d": true }}`.
- Performance suffers: 3D rendering is comparatively heavy. Narrow the visible extent or enable it only where needed.

---

## Add a Custom Data Source (Vector Tiles and More)

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/howto/custom-source/

For data too large for GeoJSON, or tiles someone else publishes, add a **tile source**. This covers raster and vector tiles served from a `{z}/{x}/{y}` template URL.

### embed

Not available with HTML attributes alone. Switch to the maps-suite or maps-react code.

### maps-suite

Wait for load, then pass `tiles`, an array of template URLs, to `addSource`. The example overlays GSI raster tiles.

```js
await map.whenReady();
const impl = map.getGeoloniaMap();
impl.addSource("gsi", {
  type: "raster",
  tiles: ["https://cyberjapandata.gsi.go.jp/xyz/pale/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"],
  tileSize: 256,
  attribution: "地理院タイル",
});
impl.addLayer({ id: "gsi", type: "raster", source: "gsi" });
```

- **`tiles`**: the tile template URL. The `{z}/{x}/{y}` part is replaced with real tile coordinates.
- **`attribution`**: the data credit. Always include the wording the publisher terms require.
- For **vector tiles**, use `type: "vector"` and give the layer a **`"source-layer"`**, the layer name inside the tile.

```js
impl.addSource("mytiles", { type: "vector", tiles: ["https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"] });
impl.addLayer({ id: "mytiles-line", type: "line", source: "mytiles", "source-layer": "roads" });
```

### maps-react

```jsx
<Source
  id="gsi"
  type="raster"
  tiles={["https://cyberjapandata.gsi.go.jp/xyz/pale/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"]}
  tileSize={256}
  attribution="地理院タイル"
>
  <Layer id="gsi-raster" type="raster" />
</Source>
```

For vector tiles, use `type="vector"` and give `Layer` a `source-layer`.

```jsx
<Source id="mytiles" type="vector" tiles={["https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"]}>
  <Layer id="mytiles-line" type="line" source-layer="roads" />
</Source>
```

The vector tile example uses a fictional `example.com` URL and will not work as written. Replace it with your own publisher.

**When it does not work**

- Nothing appears with raster: check the template URL directly in a browser. Substituting real numbers such as `12/3637/1612` and seeing whether an image comes back is the fastest check.
- Nothing appears with vector: **a mismatched `source-layer` name** is the most common cause. Confirm the exact name from the tile specification or the publisher style definition.
- Tiles are offset or coarse: check `tileSize`, which is 256 or 512 depending on the publisher.

---

## Search by Address and Show That Place

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/howto/address-search/

Deriving latitude and longitude from an address string such as "東京都千代田区大手町1-1-1" is called **geocoding**. Geolonia Maps has no geocoder of its own, so it is combined with an address library. This recipe uses `@geolonia/normalize-japanese-addresses` (NJA), at https://github.com/geolonia/normalize-japanese-addresses.

NJA is primarily an **address normalisation** library. It absorbs variation in notation, tidies the address, and also returns the coordinates of that point, which can be used on the map directly.

### What comes back

`normalize()` takes an address string and returns the decomposed address together with location information.

```js
await normalize("東京都台東区上野公園7-7");
// {
//   pref: "東京都",
//   city: "台東区",
//   town: "上野公園",
//   addr: "7-7",
//   level: 8,
//   point: { lat: 35.714952981, lng: 139.775372778, level: 8 },
//   other: "",
//   metadata: { ... }
// }
```

**`level` and `point.level` are different things.** `level` says how far into the input string could be read; `point.level` says how fine the returned coordinate is.

| level | how much was read | point.level | what the coordinate points at |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0` | not even the prefecture | | (there is no `point`) |
| `1` | prefecture | `1` | the prefectural office |
| `2` | municipality | `2` | the municipal office |
| `3` | district or block | `3` | a representative point of the district or block |
| `8` | street or house number, or a parcel number | `8` | the addressed position, or the centre of the parcel |

The two do not always agree. Even when the house number was read (`level: 8`), if that number has no location information the representative point of the district is returned (`point.level: 3`).

Match zoom to `point.level`. Zooming to level 18 on the coordinates of a municipal office reads to the viewer as "that building is that address". Varying zoom by the fineness of the coordinate is safer, and all the code below does so.

### embed

NJA is an npm package but can be loaded from a CDN as an ES module. The embed CDN script is a plain `<script>` while NJA needs `<script type="module">`. Modules execute later, so `geolonia` is already loaded.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <style>
      body { margin: 0; font: 14px/1.6 system-ui, sans-serif; }
      #wrap { display: flex; flex-direction: column; height: 100vh; }
      #search { display: flex; gap: 6px; padding: 8px; }
      #q { flex: 1; padding: 6px 8px; }
      #note { padding: 0 8px 8px; color: #555; }
      #map { flex: 1; }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="wrap">
      <form id="search">
        <input id="q" aria-label="住所" value="東京都千代田区大手町1-1-1">
        <button type="submit">検索</button>
      </form>
      <div id="note">住所を入力して検索してください。</div>
      <div id="map" data-lat="35.68" data-lng="139.76" data-zoom="8" data-marker="off"></div>
    </div>

    <script src="https://cdn.geolonia.com/embed/v5/embed?geolonia-api-key=YOUR-API-KEY"></script>
    <script type="module">
      import { normalize } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@geolonia/normalize-japanese-addresses@3.1.3/+esm";

      const ZOOM = { 1: 9, 2: 12, 3: 15, 8: 18 };

      const map = new geolonia.Map("#map");
      const marker = new geolonia.Marker();
      const note = document.getElementById("note");

      document.getElementById("search").addEventListener("submit", async (event) => {
        event.preventDefault();
        note.textContent = "検索中…";

        const result = await normalize(document.getElementById("q").value);
        if (!result.point) {
          marker.remove();
          note.textContent = "住所を特定できませんでした。";
          return;
        }

        const { lat, lng, level } = result.point;
        marker.setLngLat([lng, lat]).addTo(map);
        map.flyTo({ center: [lng, lat], zoom: ZOOM[level] });
        note.textContent =
          `${result.pref}${result.city}${result.town || ""}${result.addr || ""}` +
          `（位置情報レベル ${level}）`;
      });
    </script>
  </body>
</html>
```

- **`type="module"`**: required to load NJA from a CDN. Pinning the version avoids surprises from updates.
- **`geolonia.Marker`**: loading embed puts the contents of MapLibre GL JS on `window.geolonia`, so marker and popup classes are usable directly.
- **Whether `result.point` exists**: when the address could not be identified (`level: 0`) there is no `point`. Always check before reading it.

### maps-suite

Get the coordinates with `normalize()` and move with `panTo()` and `setZoom()`. Reuse one marker via `setPosition()`.

```js
import { normalize } from "@geolonia/normalize-japanese-addresses";
import { geolonia } from "@geolonia/maps-suite";

const ZOOM = { 1: 9, 2: 12, 3: 15, 8: 18 };

const map = new geolonia.maps.Map(container, {
  apiKey: "YOUR-API-KEY",
  center: { lat: 35.68, lng: 139.76 },
  zoom: 8,
});

const marker = new geolonia.maps.Marker();

form.addEventListener("submit", async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();

  const result = await normalize(form.querySelector("#q").value);
  if (!result.point) {
    marker.setMap(null);
    return;
  }

  const { lat, lng, level } = result.point;
  marker.setPosition({ lat, lng });
  marker.setMap(map);
  map.panTo({ lat, lng });
  map.setZoom(ZOOM[level]);
});
```

- **`setPosition()` and `setMap()`**: create one marker and move it. Calling `new` on every search leaves the previous markers behind.
- **`panTo()` and `setZoom()`**: coordinates go in as a `{ lat, lng }` object.

### maps-react

Put the search result in state and pass it to `center` and `zoom` on `Map`. Changing the values flies the map there.

```jsx
function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("東京都千代田区大手町1-1-1");
  const [found, setFound] = useState(null);

  const handleSubmit = async (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();

    const result = await normalize(query);
    if (!result.point) {
      setFound(null);
      return;
    }

    const { lat, lng, level } = result.point;
    setFound({ lat, lng, zoom: ZOOM[level] });
  };

  return (
    <Map
      apiKey="YOUR-API-KEY"
      center={found ? [found.lng, found.lat] : [139.76, 35.68]}
      zoom={found ? found.zoom : 8}
      containerStyle={{ flex: 1 }}
    >
      {found && <Marker lat={found.lat} lng={found.lng} />}
    </Map>
  );
}
```

- **`center` and `zoom`**: `Map` watches these two and moves the map. No imperative API is needed. `center` is in **`[longitude, latitude]` order**.
- **`Marker`**: `lat` and `lng` are separate props, written differently from the `center` order.

### About address data retrieval

NJA does not carry address data around; it fetches only the range it needs from a web API each time. The default endpoint is `https://japanese-addresses-v2.geoloniamaps.com/api/ja`.

- **The first call takes a moment.** It walks prefecture, then municipality, then district, so there are several network round trips. Later calls hit the browser cache.
- **It does not work offline.** For a disconnected environment, point `config.japaneseAddressesApi` at your own endpoint.
- **Failure raises an exception.** Transient failures such as 5xx, 429 and network errors are retried automatically up to twice, but anything beyond that throws. When processing in bulk, wrap calls in `try` so one failure does not stop everything.

### Can it go the other way?

No. Deriving an address from coordinates, reverse geocoding, is not something NJA does. NJA takes address strings as input.

**When it does not work**

- Nothing happens: check that you handle the case where `result.point` is absent. An unidentifiable address gives `level: 0` and no `point`.
- Accuracy drops when a building name is included: a trailing building name only remains in `other` and does not affect coordinates, but it can interfere with reading the address itself. Separating it in advance is the reliable route.
- Only a rough place appears despite giving a house number: that number has no location information and the district representative point was returned. `point.level` distinguishes the two.
- Markers accumulate with each search: you are creating a marker every time. Create one and move it.

---

## Show the Map as a Globe

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/howto/globe/

Switching the map projection to **globe** shows a globe rather than a flat map when zoomed out. Zooming in deep transitions smoothly back to the usual map display, so everyday use is unchanged.

### embed

Not available with HTML attributes alone. Switch to the maps-suite or maps-react code.

### maps-suite

Wait for load, then switch the projection with `setProjection` on the underlying map.

```js
const map = new geolonia.maps.Map(document.getElementById("map"), {
  apiKey: "YOUR-API-KEY",
  center: { lat: 20, lng: 0 },
  zoom: 2,
});

await map.whenReady();
map.getGeoloniaMap().setProjection({ type: "globe" });
```

### maps-react

Receive the map instance in `onLoad` and switch the projection.

```jsx
<Map
  apiKey="YOUR-API-KEY"
  center={[0, 20]}
  zoom={2}
  onLoad={(map) => map.setProjection({ type: "globe" })}
  containerStyle={{ width: "100%", height: "100vh" }}
/>
```

- **`setProjection({ type: "globe" })`**: switches the projection to a globe. `{ type: "mercator" }` returns to the usual flat projection.
- The tiles are the same as usual. No data or style change is needed.

**When it does not work**

- It stays flat: globe projection is a feature of **MapLibre GL JS v5 or later**. Check the `maplibre-gl` version.
- You cannot tell whether it is a globe: zoom out. At high zoom it looks the same as the usual map.

---

## Place a Map with HTML Tags Only (maps-suite)

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/howto/web-component/

maps-suite includes a custom element (Web Components) called `<geolonia-map>`. Load the CDN script and writing an HTML tag is all it takes. No JavaScript calling `new geolonia.maps.Map()` is required.

This page is about maps-suite only. embed and maps-react have no equivalent. For a single map on static HTML, embed is enough; in React, use the `<Map>` component.

### Code

`center` is a single comma-separated attribute in `"latitude,longitude"` order. The element has no height of its own, so give it one in CSS.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <style>
      geolonia-map { width: 100%; height: 100vh; }
    </style>
    <script src="https://cdn.geolonia.com/maps-suite/v1/maps-suite.js"></script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <geolonia-map
      api-key="YOUR-API-KEY"
      center="35.681236,139.767125"
      zoom="14"></geolonia-map>
  </body>
</html>
```

The script registers itself as `geolonia-map` the moment it loads, so the tag works whether it appears before or after the script.

The available attributes are:

| attribute | meaning |
|---|---|
| `api-key` | the Geolonia API key |
| `center` | initial centre, as `"latitude,longitude"` |
| `zoom` | initial zoom level |
| `map-style` | style identifier or URL |
| `map-id` | identifier of the map instance |
| `tilt-interaction-disabled` | present to disable tilt interaction |
| `heading-interaction-disabled` | present to disable rotation interaction |

### Changing attributes afterwards

Rewriting `center` and `zoom` after placement makes the map follow. Being a standard custom element, changing an attribute is enough.

```html
<button id="tokyo">東京駅</button>
<button id="osaka">大阪駅</button>
<geolonia-map
  id="map"
  api-key="YOUR-API-KEY"
  center="35.681236,139.767125"
  zoom="13"></geolonia-map>

<script>
  const el = document.getElementById("map");
  document.getElementById("tokyo").onclick = () => {
    el.setAttribute("center", "35.681236,139.767125");
  };
  document.getElementById("osaka").onclick = () => {
    el.setAttribute("center", "34.702485,135.495951");
  };
</script>
```

The embed `data-lat` and `data-lng` are read once as initial values, so this rewriting is not possible there. That is the single biggest difference between the two.

### Touching the map inside

The `innerMap` property of the element holds the maps-suite `Map` instance. Anything the attributes do not cover can be called from there.

```js
const el = document.querySelector("geolonia-map");
el.innerMap.setTilt(45);
el.innerMap.fitBounds({ north: 35.7, south: 35.6, east: 139.8, west: 139.7 }, 40);
```

For maplibre features beyond that, `getGeoloniaMap()` retrieves the underlying map.

A `geolonia-zoomchange` event is dispatched from the element when the zoom changes.

```js
el.addEventListener("geolonia-zoomchange", () => {
  console.log("zoom:", el.innerMap.getZoom());
});
```

### Fitting a server-rendered HTML setup

This approach pays off when **the server assembles the HTML and there is no bundler on the client**. Hono, for instance, returns HTML, so one `<geolonia-map>` line in the template finishes the job, touching neither the build configuration nor the npm dependencies.

```jsx
import { Hono } from "hono";

const app = new Hono();

app.get("/", (c) =>
  c.html(
    <html>
      <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8" />
        <style>{"geolonia-map { width: 100%; height: 100vh; }"}</style>
        <script src="https://cdn.geolonia.com/maps-suite/v1/maps-suite.js"></script>
      </head>
      <body>
        <geolonia-map api-key="YOUR-API-KEY" center="35.681236,139.767125" zoom="14" />
      </body>
    </html>,
  ),
);

export default app;
```

Running Hono on Cloudflare Workers, the demo key `YOUR-API-KEY` works as it is.

Custom elements are a standard mechanism, so the tag also goes straight into Vue and Svelte templates. It initialises when the element appears on screen and cleans up when it detaches, so it is safe inside conditionally rendered UI.

### Choosing between this and embed

Both put a map on the page with one CDN script and an HTML tag. The criterion is **whether the page moves**.

For a single map on static HTML, use embed. It has attributes such as `data-geojson` for loading data and `data-3d` for 3D buildings, and it takes the least writing.

Where there is movement, such as changing the map position afterwards or showing and hiding maps as tabs switch, `<geolonia-map>` fits better. It follows attribute changes, and initialisation and cleanup run as the element enters and leaves. embed scans at load time and cannot pick up maps that appear later.

**When it does not work**

- The map height is zero: give `geolonia-map` itself a height. The element has no default height.
- `center` has no effect: write it as `"latitude,longitude"`, one attribute with a comma. It is not split into separate `lat` and `lng` attributes.
- `innerMap` is `null`: you are reading it before the element enters the DOM. The map is created at the moment of insertion.
- The tag renders as plain text: the script has not loaded. Check in the network tab that `maps-suite.js` returns 200.

---

## Manage API Keys in YAML

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/howto/cli-map-keys/

API keys and the origins allowed to display maps with them can be managed in a YAML file. Since you can review what will change before applying it, this suits growing numbers of keys and teams touching them.

### Preparation

Install the Geolonia CLI, then log in and select a team.

```bash
npm install --global @geolonia/cli
geolonia login
geolonia teams select
```

### Operating one at a time

```bash
geolonia map-keys list                                   # 一覧
geolonia map-keys show <keyId>                           # 詳細
geolonia map-keys search example.com                     # 名前や許可オリジンで検索
geolonia map-keys new                                    # 新規作成
geolonia map-keys add-origin <keyId> https://example.com # 許可オリジンを足す
geolonia map-keys remove-origin <keyId> https://example.com
```

### Exporting the current state

```bash
geolonia map-keys pull -o keys.yml
```

Omitting `-o` writes to standard output. The exported shape is:

```yaml
keys:
  - name: 本番サイト
    keyId: xxxxxxxx
    userKey: YOUR-API-KEY
    origins:
      - https://example.com
      - https://www.example.com
  - name: ステージング
    keyId: yyyyyyyy
    userKey: YOUR-API-KEY
    origins:
      - https://staging.example.com
```

### Reviewing the diff

```bash
geolonia map-keys plan -f keys.yml
```

Each key is judged as follows.

| judgement | condition |
| --- | --- |
| `create` | not found by `keyId`, or not found by `name` when there is no `keyId` |
| `update` | found, but `origins` differs from the current state |
| `unchanged` | found, and `origins` matches |

Matching uses `keyId` when present and `name` otherwise. **To add a new key, write `name` and `origins` without a `keyId`.**

### Applying

```bash
geolonia map-keys apply -f keys.yml
```

Keys marked `create` are created, and keys marked `update` have their `origins` brought in line with the YAML, adding what is missing and removing what is extra. With no diff it prints `No changes required.` and does nothing.

**Only origins are applied.** What `apply` reconciles is the allowed origins. Rewriting `name` in the YAML does not necessarily rename the key, so use the dashboard or an individual command when you want to change a name.

**Keys cannot be deleted.** `geolonia map-keys delete <keyId>` exists but is disabled for safety. Removing a key entry from the YAML will not delete that key, because deleting a key stops every map using it at once.

### Putting the file in a repository

`keys.yml` holds key names, IDs, public keys and allowed origins. All of that is public information used in serving maps, so committing it is fine.

By contrast `~/.config/geolonia/credential.yml` holds a refresh token. **Never put that in a repository.**

---

## Explanation

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/explanation/

The Explanation section collects the concepts worth knowing when using Geolonia Maps, and the background to why certain parts are the way they are.

### Why MapLibre GL JS compatible?

Rather than learning a closed proprietary API, **knowledge of a standard map API used worldwide applies directly**. The official documentation is readable, the knowledge does not go to waste, and migration is easier. When stuck, search for "how would MapLibre write this". That is the learning strategy compatibility buys.

### What vector tiles are

A mechanism that divides map data into square tiles and serves only the range needed. Vector tiles in particular carry the data itself, "this is a road", rather than a picture, so they do not blur when zoomed and their appearance (the style) can be changed afterwards.

### What a map style is

What decides the appearance of a map is the style. Because data and appearance are separate, the same data yields both a light map and a dark one.

### Icons available for marker-symbol

The names writable in the GeoJSON `marker-symbol` are decided by the icons contained in the map style, not by type definitions. Usable names therefore change with the style.

### What Geolonia Agent Skills is

A Claude Code plugin for having an AI coding agent help with development that uses Geolonia Maps.

---

## What a Map Style Is

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/explanation/map-style/

A **style** is a JSON file describing how to draw map data. What colour to fill the sea, how many pixels wide to draw a road, whether to omit station names below zoom 12. Those drawing rules are gathered in it.

What you specify in Geolonia Maps as `geolonia/basic-v2` is the name of such a style.

### Data and appearance are separate

On a paper map, the terrain information and the printed colours are one thing. Rewriting means reprinting.

On a vector tile map the two are separate. Map data is served carrying attributes such as "this is a road" and "this is water", and colours and widths are decided afterwards by the style. From the same data you can build both a light map and a dark one.

Only the style is reloaded, so switching appearance does not refetch the data.

### What is inside a style

The style JSON holds three broad kinds of information.

- **sources**: where data comes from. The URLs serving the vector tiles.
- **layers**: drawing rules. Which data, at which scale, in which colour and width, listed one by one.
- **glyphs and sprite**: the letterforms for text and the images for icons.

`layers` is the substance. `geolonia/basic-v2` has 139 layers. Sea, rivers, greenery, buildings, the lines for each road class, station names and place names are each handled by a separate layer.

The format of this JSON is defined by the MapLibre Style Spec and is not a Geolonia-specific format. Styles usable with MapLibre GL JS work as they are, and MapLibre materials are readable when researching how to write a style.

### Specifying a style

There are two ways.

A **logical name** is a short name such as `geolonia/basic-v2`. Styles Geolonia provides are specified this way. Omitting the specification uses `geolonia/basic-v2`.

A **URL** points directly at a style.json, for styles published elsewhere or written yourself.

```html
<div class="geolonia"
     data-lat="35.68" data-lng="139.75" data-zoom="11"
     data-style="geolonia/midnight"></div>
```

### Writing your own style

When an existing style is not enough, a style you wrote yourself can be specified by URL. Besides writing JSON directly, editors such as Maputnik can be used.

To start from a Geolonia style, fetch `https://cdn.geolonia.com/style/geolonia/basic-v2/ja.json` and modify it. Note that the API key contained in the `sources` URLs has to be replaced with your own.

---

## Geolonia Maps Style List

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/explanation/styles/

The styles Geolonia officially provides. Pass the logical name to `data-style` or `style` to switch.

| logical name | contents |
|---|---|
| `geolonia/basic-v2` | the standard style, used when the specification is omitted |
| `geolonia/gsi` | a style using the vector tiles of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan |
| `geolonia/midnight` | a dark style based on deep navy |
| `geolonia/red-planet` | a style based on dark red |
| `geolonia/notebook` | a pale style based on white |
| `geolonia/homework` | a simple worldwide style from Natural Earth |
| `geoloniamaps/smartcity-base` | a style using the optimised vector tiles of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan |

There are also two deprecated styles.

- **`geolonia/basic-v2`**: the standard style, based on OpenStreetMap data.
- **`geolonia/gsi`**: uses the vector tiles of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan, so representation within Japan resembles the GSI maps.
- **`geolonia/midnight`**: dark, based on deep navy. Useful over a dark screen, or under strongly coloured data.
- **`geolonia/red-planet`**: based on dark red.
- **`geolonia/notebook`**: pale, based on white. Suited to keeping the map itself quiet so that overlaid data leads.
- **`geolonia/homework`**: a simple worldwide style using Natural Earth, built from only 9 layers, centred on borders and country names. It contains no blocks or roads, so it is unsuited to zooming into Japan.
- **`geoloniamaps/smartcity-base`**: reads the optimised vector tiles of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan in PMTiles format. It is the only style whose logical name begins with `geoloniamaps/`.

### Deprecated styles

The following two are older styles superseded by `geolonia/basic-v2`. They are still served and will work if specified, but use `geolonia/basic-v2` for new work. The vector tiles they reference differ from those of `basic-v2`.

- **`geolonia/basic`**: the original standard style. It includes the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries parcel polygons (farmland plots), so zooming into rural areas shows plot boundaries.
- **`geolonia/basic-v1`**: the previous generation standard style. Its palette is close to `basic-v2`, but the vector tiles it references differ.

### Language

Each style has a Japanese and an English version, changing the language of labels such as place names. Switch with the `data-lang` attribute or the `lang` option.

---

## Icons Available for marker-symbol

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/explanation/marker-symbol/

Writing a name in the GeoJSON `marker-symbol` draws the marker with an icon contained in the map style.

```json
{
  "type": "Feature",
  "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [139.767125, 35.681236] },
  "properties": {
    "marker-symbol": "park"
  }
}
```

The list on this page is assembled at build time from the sprite JSON of the style, using `geolonia/basic-v2` as the baseline, which is the default style the examples in this documentation use. Because the usable names come from the style rather than from type definitions, they change when the style changes.

---

## Environments Where the Demo Key Works

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/explanation/free-referers/

The `YOUR-API-KEY` appearing throughout the documentation and samples is a **demo key** that lets you try maps without issuing one. Only for access from pre-approved environments (domains) does a map render without a real API key. The point is to make the order "get it running first, obtain a key when publishing" possible.

### Where it works

The allowed domains are set for environments commonly used during development and prototyping. Representative ones follow, though this is not the complete set.

**Local development**

- `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`, on any port
- Development domains such as `*.test`, `*.local` and `*.example`

**Online editors and playgrounds**

- CodePen (`codepen.io`)
- CodeSandbox (`*.csb.app`)
- JSFiddle
- PlayCode

**Free hosting and previews**

- GitHub Pages (`*.github.io`)
- Netlify (`*.netlify.app`)
- Vercel (`*.vercel.app`)
- Cloudflare Pages and Workers (`*.pages.dev` and `*.workers.dev`)

So pasting into CodePen, or deploying straight to GitHub Pages, Netlify or Vercel, displays a map for checking without waiting for a key.

### Production publishing needs a real key

The demo key works only on such "try it and prototype" environments. To publish on your own domain such as `example.com`, issue a production API key on the Geolonia dashboard at https://app.geolonia.com/ and register the domain you will use.

Allowed domains are updated from time to time, so the above is an excerpt of the main ones. The complete list is in `referers.json` at https://github.com/geolonia/free-referers/blob/master/referers.json.

---

## What the Geolonia CLI Is

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/explanation/cli/

**Geolonia CLI** is the official tool for operating things in your Geolonia account from the command line. Its role differs from the map-drawing libraries (embed, maps-suite, maps-react); this one handles **the preparation and operation that comes before drawing a map**.

Two things are available today.

- **API key management**: creating keys, adding and removing allowed origins, exporting the configuration to YAML and applying it after reviewing the diff.
- **Plan and usage checks**: the current plan, this month's map display count, and the quota.

The dashboard can do the same things. What the CLI suits is **wanting the procedure to be reproducible**, such as writing the key configuration to a file and applying it after reviewing the diff.

### Installing

Node.js is required, **version 22.0.0 or later**.

```bash
npm install --global @geolonia/cli
```

```bash
geolonia --version
```

### Logging in and selecting a team

Every command assumes you are logged in and that a target team is selected.

```bash
geolonia login
geolonia teams select
```

`geolonia teams select` lists the teams you belong to and asks for a number. If you know the team ID, pass it directly as `geolonia teams select <teamId>`.

```bash
geolonia whoami
```

### Where configuration and credentials live

| file | contents |
| --- | --- |
| `~/.config/geolonia/credential.yml` | user name and refresh token |
| `~/.config/geolonia/config.yml` | the selected team |

Both can be pointed elsewhere with `--credential-file` and `--config-file`, which is useful for switching between several teams or accounts on one machine.

`credential.yml` holds a refresh token. Do not include it in a repository or leave it on a shared machine.

### Command list

| command | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `geolonia login` | log in and save the token |
| `geolonia teams list` | list the teams you belong to |
| `geolonia teams select [teamId]` | select the team to operate on |
| `geolonia user show` / `whoami` / `me` | show the current user information |
| `geolonia map-keys list` | list API keys |
| `geolonia map-keys show <keyId>` | show the details of an API key |
| `geolonia map-keys search <query>` | search keys by name or allowed origin |
| `geolonia map-keys new` | create a new API key |
| `geolonia map-keys add-origin <keyId> <origin>` | add an allowed origin |
| `geolonia map-keys remove-origin <keyId> <origin>` | remove an allowed origin |
| `geolonia map-keys pull` | export the current key configuration to YAML |
| `geolonia map-keys plan -f <file>` | show the diff between the YAML and the current state |
| `geolonia map-keys apply -f <file>` | apply the contents of the YAML |
| `geolonia plan show` | show the current plan, this month's map display count and the quota |
| `geolonia plan list` | list the available plans |
| `geolonia generate-access-token` | issue a team access token |

`geolonia map-keys delete <keyId>` exists, but running it **only tells you to delete the key from the dashboard**, because deleting a key stops every map using it at once.

`geolonia plan show` and `geolonia plan list` require **0.4.0 or later**. Older versions report `unknown command 'plan'`.

### Viewing plan and usage

```bash
geolonia plan show
```

Shows the current plan, this month's map display count and the quota for the selected team, without opening the dashboard.

```bash
geolonia plan list
```

Lists the available plans with their names, prices, included map display counts and member limits. **This is the one command that needs no login**, so plans can be compared before contracting.

### Using it from CI

`geolonia generate-access-token` issues a team access token from the saved refresh token. It is intended for environments where interactive login is impossible, such as CI, passing the token through an environment variable.

---

## What Geolonia Agent Skills Is

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/explanation/agent-skills/

**Geolonia Agent Skills** is a plugin for having Claude Code (https://code.claude.com/) help build map applications with Geolonia Maps. It is neither a map-drawing library nor a tool for operating your account. It is **a way of teaching the agent how Geolonia Maps is written**.

This documentation is written for people to read. Think of the plugin as the same content reorganised into a form an agent can read and use.

| what you use | its role |
| --- | --- |
| embed, maps-suite, maps-react | drawing maps |
| Geolonia CLI | managing API keys, checking plan and usage |
| Geolonia Agent Skills | having an agent write the map code |

It is distributed at https://github.com/geolonia/geolonia-agent-skills under the MIT licence.

### Why it is needed

Agents are not ignorant of Geolonia Maps, but they write from the knowledge they had at training time. That produces drift such as:

- writing deprecated style names or old CDN paths
- applying MapLibre GL JS idioms directly and missing the Geolonia conventions
- treating a feature that **already exists** in maps-suite as absent and writing a roundabout workaround

The skills hand these premises to the agent on the spot. Instead of pasting them into every prompt, they are loaded only when needed.

### The skills included

**maps** supports building map applications with Geolonia Maps.

- **Embed API**: declarative map embedding through HTML `data-*` attributes
- **JavaScript API**: working with `geolonia.Map`, `Marker`, `Popup` and `SimpleStyle`
- **Geocoding**: address to coordinates, coordinates to address, and Japanese address normalisation
- **Map styles**: the list of built-in styles and how to customise them

Setup is standardised on CDN embedding.

**geolonia-google-maps-migration** supports migration from the Google Maps JavaScript API to `@geolonia/maps-suite`. It carries the procedure from inventory through installation, obtaining an API key, initialising the map, moving markers and info windows over, and building and verifying.

A correspondence table between `google.maps.*` and `geolonia.maps.*`, the APIs that differ in detail, and the gaps not yet filled along with their workarounds, are split across reference files.

### Requirements and installation

Claude Code **v1.0.33 or later** is required. Add the marketplace, then install.

```text
/plugin marketplace add geolonia/geolonia-agent-skills
/plugin install geolonia@geolonia
```

### Using it

Ask for anything map-related and the agent loads the skills it needs by itself.

```text
「Geolonia Maps で東京タワーにマーカーを置いた地図を作って」
```

To invoke one explicitly, use the slash command.

```text
/geolonia:maps
```

### How it is structured

Rather than one file, a skill is split into an entry point `SKILL.md` and reference files read only when needed, so that the agent does not have to read everything up front.

```text
skills/
├── maps/
│   ├── SKILL.md               # 入口。いつ使うか、基本の方針
│   ├── embed-api.md           # data-* 属性の一覧
│   ├── javascript-api.md      # JavaScript API
│   ├── geocoding.md           # 住所と座標の変換、住所正規化
│   ├── styles.md              # スタイル一覧とカスタマイズ
│   └── examples.md            # よくあるパターンのコード例
└── geolonia-google-maps-migration/
    ├── SKILL.md               # 入口。移行手順
    ├── AGENTS.md              # 凝縮版のクイックリファレンス
    └── references/
        ├── known-gaps.md      # まだ無い機能と回避策
        ├── api-differences.md # 細部が異なる API
        ├── marker-icons.md    # マーカーアイコン
        └── shapes.md          # 図形の移行
```

### It tracks the library version

This is the part of the plugin that needs the most care.

The content of the skills, and in particular the "gaps not yet filled and their workarounds" in the migration skill, **is written against a specific version of `@geolonia/maps-suite`**. When the library gains a feature, the workaround becomes nothing but a detour. `Polyline`, `Polygon` and `Circle`, absent from the early versions, were added later.

To avoid having old workarounds written, observe the following.

- Check **the stated target version** at the top of each reference file.
- When it disagrees with the version of `@geolonia/maps-suite` you use, pull the latest from the repository again.
- If generated code uses a `_getImpl()` workaround, check whether the current version has an official API for it.

The repository is always the source of truth.

### Trying and fixing it locally

Clone the repository and load it directly with `--plugin-dir`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/geolonia/geolonia-agent-skills.git
cd /path/to/your-project
claude --plugin-dir /path/to/geolonia-agent-skills
```

Restarting Claude Code applies edits to the skill files. The structure can be validated with:

```bash
claude plugin validate /path/to/geolonia-agent-skills
```

---

## Reference

URL: https://docs.geolonia.com/reference/

API reference generated from the type definitions of each library. The generated pages themselves are not reproduced in this file.

### @geolonia/embed

The library that displays a map with only a `<script>` tag and a `<div>` tag, configured through `data-*` attributes. See https://docs.geolonia.com/reference/embed/.

`EmbedAttributes` carries the complete list of `data-*` attributes and their defaults. For writing plugins, see `EmbedPlugin`.

### @geolonia/maps-suite

The library that drives the map imperatively from JavaScript, with classes and types under the `geolonia.maps` namespace. See https://docs.geolonia.com/reference/suite/geolonia.Namespace.maps/.

Besides `Map` and `Marker` there are `InfoWindow` and `MarkerClusterer`, shapes such as `Circle` and `Polygon`, and value types such as `LatLng` and `LatLngBounds`. To draw GeoJSON with mixed geometry types in one go, there is the `Data` layer reached from `Map.data`.

### @geolonia/maps-react

The React library. **This is the only library without a reference generated from type definitions.** Most of its props are taken straight from maps-core, so `GeoloniaMapOptions` in the maps-core reference is the list of `Map` options, minus `container`. `GeoloniaMapOptions` is the MapLibre GL JS `MapOptions` type plus Geolonia-specific entries, so most map initialisation options are covered by the MapLibre documentation.

`Map` additionally has props deciding the appearance of the container such as `containerStyle` and `className`, props receiving map events such as `onClick` and `onMoveEnd`, `interactiveLayerIds` for narrowing which layers are clickable, and `onLoad` for retrieving the map instance. These are maps-react additions and do not appear on the MapLibre side.

The available components are `Map` for the map itself, `Source` and `Layer` for data and drawing, `Marker` and `Popup`, and the controls (`NavigationControl`, `GeolocateControl`, `FullscreenControl`, `ScaleControl`, `AttributionControl`, and `Control` for writing your own). There is also `MapProvider` for handling several maps together, along with hooks such as `useMap`.

What you pass to `Source` and `Layer` is the MapLibre GL JS source and layer definition as it is. What can be written in `paint` and `layout`, and how `filter` expressions work, is covered by the MapLibre GL JS documentation. The map instance received in `onLoad` also extends the MapLibre `Map`, so the same documentation applies.

### @geolonia/maps-core

The shared foundation of the three libraries above. It is essentially MapLibre GL JS with Geolonia map access and conveniences added. See https://docs.geolonia.com/reference/core/.

At its core, `GeoloniaMap` is **the MapLibre GL JS `Map` class extended to work with Geolonia maps**, covering API key handling, style name resolution and the default controls. MapLibre features such as `flyTo()`, `addLayer()` and `on()` are therefore available as they are. Only what Geolonia added appears in the reference, so **for the inherited API see the MapLibre GL JS documentation**, particularly the `Map` class reference at https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/API/classes/Map/. The supported line is MapLibre GL JS v5.

The reference covers the map itself as `GeoloniaMap` and its options `GeoloniaMapOptions`, plus `GeoloniaMarker` and `SimpleStyle`, which applies styling to GeoJSON.
